title: Carpet to Hardwood Transitions: How Pros Finish the Edge
meta: Carpet to hardwood transitions done right: tack strip set back, carpet tucked into the gully, no metal strip unless heights differ. Wills Flooring, Edmonds.
keywords: carpet to hardwood transition, how to transition carpet to hardwood floor, carpet to wood floor transition strip, tuck carpet edge against hardwood, carpet hardwood doorway transition, carpet installation Edmonds

blocks.lead: A professional carpet-to-hardwood transition has no visible metal at all: the tack strip is set back from the hardwood by about the thickness of the carpet, the pad stops at the strip, and the carpet edge is stretched, trimmed and tucked down into that gully so it meets the wood as a clean, tight seam.
blocks.detail: Metal strips, Z-bars and wood reducers are for when the two floors sit at different heights or the carpet has to be held on a hard surface. In most Edmonds homes, where 3/4 in oak meets carpet over pad, the tuck is the right finish. It is also part of the $0.99 per sq ft installation labor, not an extra line.

blocks.html: Walk through a 1960s Seaview or Westgate rambler and you find the same detail at every bedroom door: gold or silver metal where the hallway oak meets the bedroom carpet, usually bent, usually with fuzz pulling out of it. Homeowners assume that strip is required. It is not. It was the fast way to finish an edge, and it is the first thing we remove when we recarpet. Here is how a good crew finishes that edge.

blocks.text: What is actually happening at the edge

items.title: The tack strip
items.text: A wood strip with angled pins, nailed to the subfloor parallel to the hardwood edge. It holds the carpet under tension. Where it sits decides everything: too close and there is no room to tuck, too far and the edge sags into a gap.

items.title: The gully
items.text: The gap between the tack strip and the hardwood, a little less than the carpet's thickness, usually 1/4 to 3/8 in. The trimmed edge is pushed into it with a stair tool, so the cut disappears and the pile stands flush against the wood.

items.title: The pad
items.text: Cushion stops at the inside edge of the tack strip and is stapled there, never running under the strip or into the gully. Pad in the gully is why some transitions feel spongy and let the carpet pull loose.

items.title: The trim cut
items.text: The carpet is stretched onto the pins first, then cut with a wall trimmer leaving just enough to tuck. Cut short and the backing shows, cut long and the edge bunches and wears. This step separates a tight seam from a fuzzy one.

blocks.text: The four ways to finish the edge, and when each is right

What it looks like
rows: Carpet over pad meeting 3/4 in hardwood at roughly the same height. The standard in Edmonds ramblers.
No hardware. Carpet pile meets the wood edge in a straight line.
Carpet that must end on a hard surface with no room for tack strip, such as a slab hallway or a tile edge.
A thin metal lip pinches the carpet edge; nearly invisible when done well.
Rentals, commercial edges, or very thin carpet that will not tuck cleanly.
The visible metal strip most people picture. Durable but dated.
Carpet meeting a floor that is noticeably higher or lower, or a doorway where two floors need a defined stop.
A sloped wood piece matched to the hardwood; the carpet tucks against it.
blocks.note: Any of these can be done well or badly. The failures in older Edmonds homes are almost always bent binder bars and gullies cut too wide.

blocks.text: Where the transition goes, room by room

items.d: Bedroom doorways off a hardwood hall
items.text: The seam sits under the closed door, so the hall shows wood and the room shows carpet. Hinge jamb to latch jamb, straight, not angled.
items.note: If the old metal strip left nail holes in the oak, we fill them before tucking.

items.d: Top of a carpeted staircase meeting a hardwood landing
items.text: The carpet wraps the top nosing and tucks to a tack strip on the landing side, or ends at a reducer on a hardwood landing. Never a metal bar at the top step; that is a trip point.
items.note: Common in Perrinville and Seaview split-entries.

items.d: Open living room to carpeted family room
items.text: With no door to hide under, the seam goes at the narrowest point of the opening and stays perfectly straight. Run the pile toward the opening so it does not throw a shadow line.
items.note: We snap a line on the subfloor before the tack strip goes down.

items.d: Carpet meeting hardwood at a step-down
items.text: Where a 1970s sunken living room drops to carpet, the hardwood edge gets a nosing or bullnose and the carpet tucks beneath it. Nothing to catch a toe.
items.note: Older Edmonds owners downsizing into ramblers ask about this one most.

blocks.text: When the tuck is the wrong choice

a.title: The clean tuck works when
items: Hardwood and carpet-plus-pad finish within about 1/4 in of each other
There is a wood subfloor to nail tack strip into
The edge is straight and under a door or at a natural room break

b.title: Choose a reducer or Z-bar when
items: The height difference is more than about 3/8 in; a tuck leaves a soft ledge
Carpet ends on concrete, tile or a slab where tack strip cannot go
A loose berber or wool loop is likely to unravel at a raw cut edge

blocks.title: Edmonds moisture note:
blocks.text: Homes in the Bowl and along the waterfront run humid. Hardwood edges swell slightly in winter, so on summer installs we keep the gully at the tighter end of the range and never force a reducer hard against the carpet. A transition tight in August and loose in February was cut wrong.
Mistakes we fix in Edmonds houses every month

items.html: Metal binder bar at every door. Standard in 1970s builder installs, it reads as a rental finish now and the edges bend up. Replace it with a tuck when you recarpet.
Gully too wide. With the strip 3/4 in or more from the wood, the edge has nothing to press against, sags, and the backing shows as a dark line.
Pad run under the tack strip. The strip floats, the pins lose bite, and the carpet creeps back from the wood within a year.
Tack strip nailed into the hardwood. Some installers set the strip on the oak itself to close a gap. It splits boards and ruins the edge for the next refinish.
Raw edge not sealed. On loop and wool the cut edge should be latex-sealed before tucking, or it frays at the door within months.
Sun-faded oak under the old strip. Pull a metal bar and you find a pale stripe where the wood never saw light. Only a refinish of the hall blends it, so plan both together.

faq.q: Do you need a transition strip between carpet and hardwood?
faq.a: Not usually. When carpet over pad meets 3/4 in hardwood at roughly the same height, the professional finish is to tuck the edge into a gully beside a tack strip, with no hardware at all. A metal or wood transition is needed only when the floors differ in height or the carpet ends on concrete or tile.

faq.q: Where should the carpet to hardwood transition be in a doorway?
faq.a: Directly under the door when it is closed, so each room shows one floor. The seam runs straight from the hinge jamb to the latch jamb. In a wide opening with no door, put it at the narrowest point and snap a line so it stays perfectly straight.

faq.q: Why does my carpet edge pull away from the hardwood?
faq.a: Three common causes: the tack strip set too far from the wood, so the edge had nothing to press against; pad run under the strip, so the pins lost grip; or carpet that was never properly stretched before trimming. All three are installer errors, and all three turn up in older Edmonds homes.

faq.q: Can carpet be tucked against hardwood without a tack strip?
faq.a: No. The strip is what holds the carpet under tension at the edge. Gluing an edge to the wood or subfloor is a temporary fix that fails and leaves adhesive on the oak. With no wood subfloor to nail into, a Z-bar or glue-down tack strip does the job instead.

faq.q: Can you remove the old metal strips when you recarpet?
faq.a: Yes, and we recommend it. We pull the bar, fill the nail holes, set new tack strip at the correct setback and tuck the new carpet, all inside the $0.99 per sq ft labor. If the wood under the old bar is paler than the rest of the hall, only a refinish blends it.
